about: HI (Iona), 793-1066: Columba's island, mother of Lindisfarne, in its last quiet summers and through what comes after. One port. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/hi.md, the spine and Design/content/realms/irish_sea.md; a draft for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what is not checked; 'invented' marks what the sources do not give. The name 'Iona' is never said in these years: the island is Hi, or I of Colum Cille. Woven with the region on 7 Oct 2026: the abbots Feradach and Mugrón and a Norse-born brother made real; Amlaíb Cuarán is one person now, under duiblinn.amlaib_cuaran in duiblinn.json; ties run both ways, beats pointed at their cards (Data/encounters/northumbria_irish_sea_793.json).

ports.summary: A low green island with one hill, a mile of shallow sound between it and the pink rocks of Mull, and on its east shore the mother house of all Columba's churches: a timber church, cells, a writing house and a guest house inside a great bank and ditch. Nothing is bought or sold here and no coin is struck within three hundred sea miles. A merchant comes as the abbot's guest, with wine for the Mass, calfskin, colours, iron, salt and timber, and leaves with a blessing, sealskin, a letter, the abbot's protection in every land that honours the saint, and news that will be written down. In June 793 nobody here has yet seen a heathen sail.
ports.seasons: The year turns on Colum Cille's feast, the ninth of June, when boats come from every house of his family, and on Adomnan's, the twenty-third of September, after the reaping on the western plain. Wednesdays and Fridays are fasts, broken for a guest. The seals pup on their islet at the back of the year, the cranes and geese come over from Ireland on the west wind, and from November to Brigit's day the Sound is often shut by weather for a week at a time. From 794 the brothers count the summer by the days nothing came out of the north.

history.text: Columba comes over from Ireland with twelve companions and founds his house on the island.
history.source: en.wikipedia Iona Abbey; Adomnan, Life of Saint Columba (Reeves 1874)

history.text: Columba dies on the ninth of June before the altar, after copying the psalter to the foot of a page and blessing the island from the little hill. His stone pillow is kept by his grave.
history.source: Adomnan, Life of Saint Columba III.23 (Reeves 1874); Design/content/lore/texts_more.json adamnan_last_page

history.text: About this year Aidan is sent from Hi at King Oswald's asking, and Lindisfarne is founded as a daughter of this house.
history.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.3; Design/content/dossiers/lindisfarena.md

history.text: Abbot Adomnan's law is proclaimed: the fines for killing or carrying off women, clerics and children are owed to the community of Hi. It is renewed in 727.
history.source: en.wikipedia Cain Adomnain; Design/content/realms/irish_sea.json

history.text: The house gives up its own reckoning of Easter and its old tonsure and takes Rome's.
history.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History V.22; Design/content/lore/saints_calendar.md

history.text: About this year the record of each year's events, kept on the island since Columba's time, is carried on elsewhere. The annals of Ireland grow from it.
history.source: en.wikipedia Chronicle of Ireland

history.text: Bresal son of Segene becomes abbot, the successor of Colum Cille. He holds the island for thirty-one years.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 801.4 (chronicle_793.json 801-bresal); en.wikipedia Abbot of Iona

history.text: Niall Frossach, who had been king of Tara, dies on the island as a pilgrim. Artgal of Connacht does the same in 791.
history.source: dossier hi.md section 1, from memory of the Annals of Ulster (?)

history.text: Donncoirce, king of Dal Riata, dies. After him nobody can say for sure who is king over the island's own people.
history.source: en.wikipedia Dal Riata

history.text: This year all the islands of Britain are wasted by heathens.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 794.7 (Design/content/realms/irish_sea.json); en.wikipedia Scandinavian Scotland

history.text: Hi is plundered for the first time. Skye and Rechru are struck the same summer.
history.source: Annals of Inisfallen 795.2 (chronicle_793.json 795-iona-plundered)

history.text: Bresal dies in the thirty-first year of his abbacy. Suibne, who gave up the abbacy in 771, dies the same year.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 801.4 (chronicle_793.json 801-bresal); en.wikipedia Abbot of Iona

history.text: Hi is burned by heathens. Abbot Connachtach, a choice scribe, dies. Cellach son of Congal follows him.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 802.9 (chronicle_793.json 802-iona-burned); en.wikipedia Abbot of Iona; 'choice scribe' from memory (?)

history.text: Kells in Ireland is given to the community of Colum Cille without a battle.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 804.12 (chronicle_793.json 804-kells-given)

history.text: Sixty-eight of the community of Hi are killed by heathens. The annal does not say where on the island they died.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 806.8 (chronicle_793.json 806-iona-68-killed); en.wikipedia Iona Abbey

history.text: The building of the new house of Colum Cille at Kells is begun. It is finished in 814; Cellach gives up the abbacy and Diarmait, fosterling of Daigre, takes it. Cellach dies the next year.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 807.4, 814.9 (chronicle_793.json 807-kells-monastery, 814-cellach-resigns)

history.text: Diarmait goes to Alba with the relics of Colum Cille; again in 829; and to Ireland with them in 831.
history.source: en.wikipedia Diarmait of Iona; Design/content/realms/irish_sea.json

history.text: Blathmac son of Flann, a king's son turned monk, is killed by heathens on the island. A Frankish abbot far away by the Rhine puts it in verse: he had the shrine buried under turf, said Mass, would not tell, and was cut down.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 825.17 (Design/content/realms/irish_sea.json); en.wikipedia Blathmac; Walafrid Strabo's poem, not opened (?)

history.text: The relics of Colum Cille are shared. Abbot Indrechtach brings some to Ireland; King Kenneth takes some to Dunkeld. Indrechtach is killed among the English on his way to Rome on 12 March 854.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 849.7, 854.3 (Design/content/realms/irish_sea.json); en.wikipedia Indrechtach ua Finnachta, Kenneth MacAlpin

history.text: The shrine of Colum Cille and his other relics are taken to Ireland in flight from the foreigners. An abbot and monks remain on the island.
history.source: en.wikipedia Abbey of Kells; Annals of Ulster 878.9, from memory (?); en.wikipedia Abbot of Iona

history.text: Mael Brigte son of Tornan dies on 22 February, successor of Patrick and of Colum Cille together. He sat at Armagh, not on the island.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 927.1 (Design/content/realms/irish_sea.json); en.wikipedia Abbot of Iona

history.text: After his sons are beaten at Tara, Amlaib Cuaran, king of the foreigners of Dublin, comes to Hi in penance and dies here, this year or the next.
history.source: Annals of Tigernach 980 (Design/content/realms/irish_sea.json; chronicle_793.json 980-tara); en.wikipedia Amlaib Cuaran

history.text: On Christmas night Danes plunder Hi and kill the abbot, Mael Ciarain, and fifteen elders of the house. About this time a bag of some three hundred and fifty pennies, mostly English, is hidden on the island and never fetched.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 986.3 (Design/content/realms/irish_sea.json); en.wikipedia Abbot of Iona; the hoard from memory (?)

history.text: Three hundred and sixty of those who plundered Hi are killed.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 987.3 (Design/content/realms/irish_sea.json)

history.text: At Kells the great Gospel of Colum Cille is stolen by night for the sake of its shrine. It is found months later under a sod, its gold gone.
history.source: Annals of Ulster 1007.11 (Design/content/realms/irish_sea.json); en.wikipedia Book of Kells

history.text: Abbot Flandabra dies. Abbots are on the island before him and after him, to the end of the century.
history.source: en.wikipedia Abbot of Iona

eras.text: The quiet end of a long peace. Bresal is very old, the house is full, the writing house is busy and the news from Lindisfarne is a thing that happened to a daughter far away. Guests are washed, fed and asked for news. Nobody keeps a watch.

The years of the sails. Plundered in 795, burned in 802, and in 806 sixty-eight dead. The church is rebuilt each time, in timber and then in stone (?); a brother sits on the hill from Easter to Michaelmas; the best books and vessels are kept packed. The house still receives guests, and wants timber, iron and hulls more than wine.

The house is two houses. The abbot is mostly at Kells in Ireland and the treasures cross the sea in small boats; the island keeps its graves, its crosses, a smaller company of stubborn men and, some summers, the saint's shrine. The strict clients of God set the tone under Diarmait: more fasting, fewer words. In 825 Blathmac dies for the shrine.

A small company on a famous rock. The Hebrides are full of little fleets until about 840 and a careful master stays away. In 849 the relics are shared between Kells and Dunkeld; in 878 the shrine goes to Ireland. Pilgrims still come to the grave, and kings ask to lie in the graveyard.

Quiet, poor and holy. The man who calls himself Columba's successor sits in Ireland; the island has its own head and a dozen or two of brothers (?). The lords of the sea round it are Northmen who have begun to be baptised, and their dead start to come to Oran's ground with crosses on their stones. Silver is weighed in rings and cut pieces.

A hard decade. An old king of Dublin dies here in sackcloth; six years later, on Christmas night, Danes kill the abbot and fifteen elders. The next year the killers are killed. Keep south of the island in 986 and 987 unless you have a strong reason.

An island among the kings of the Isles and the earls of Orkney (?), who honour it. Norse and Irish are both spoken on the beach, a rune stone lies among the cross slabs, and English and Dublin pennies turn up in alms. The stone abbey a later age will know is not built: it is still thatch, turf, a small stone chapel and the old crosses.

sites.name: The port of the island
sites.see: A curve of white shell sand on the east shore, the water over it green as glass and so clear the keel's shadow runs ahead of the boat. Hide boats lie bottom up above the weed line with stones on their gunwales; one wooden boat sits on rollers. Behind, a turf bank as high as a house, thatch above it, and the tops of tall stone crosses. Across the Sound the rocks of Mull are pink in the evening. It smells of weed, peat smoke and wet hide.
sites.source: Boats lie on the sand of the east shore below the monastery, no quay known (dossier hi.md 1); the Sound: white sand, pink granite on the Mull side (Research/water_levels/ireland_isles.md)

sites.name: The shouting place
sites.see: The narrowest water, a mile of it, with low islets in the stream and the tide running a slow walking pace. On the far rocks a figure cups his hands and shouts; long after, the sound arrives. A brother pushes a hide boat down the sand without hurry. Terns work the tide line and a seal watches from the slack.
sites.source: People on the Mull shore shout across the Sound and a boat is sent: Adomnan, Life of Columba I.20 and elsewhere (Reeves 1874, numbers not re-checked (?)); en.wikipedia Sound of Iona

sites.name: The guest house inside the bank
sites.see: A long low house of wattle and thatch just inside the gap in the great bank, its door to the south. In front, a wooden tub and a brother with his sleeves rolled, waiting to wash a stranger's feet whether the stranger likes it or not. Inside: a peat fire on a flat stone, benches, a pot of barley and milk, a pilgrim asleep with his boots on. Wednesday and Friday there is no meat, until a guest comes; then there is.
sites.source: The guest house made ready and water drawn to wash the strangers' feet: Adomnan I.4; the fast broken for a guest: I.20 (Reeves 1874, as cited in dossier hi.md 2, 6). The vallum: Historic Environment Scotland, Iona Abbey

sites.name: The kiln and the barn
sites.see: A round drying kiln with a wisp of smoke and a long barn beside it, the door wide enough for two men with a cask on a pole. Here is where a cargo is looked at: wine tasted from a horn spoon, iron rung against a stone, salt rubbed between finger and thumb. Nothing is priced. The guest-master says what the house needs, and afterwards what the house gives, and a boy cuts both on a stick. A white horse stands at the door with empty milk pails.
sites.source: Adomnan names a kiln, a barn, the grinding of corn and a white horse that carried the milk pails (I.35 (?), III.23, as in dossier hi.md 2). No market, toll or sale is recorded: a house that receives (dossier 4). Worth in cows and ounces of silver: Design/content/realms/irish_sea.md

sites.name: The church of Colum Cille
sites.see: A timber church, steep-roofed, its planks grey with a hundred winters and its door facing the crosses; after the burning of 802 a smaller one, and then walls of stone (?). Inside it is dark and warm: one lamp, a stone altar, a book on it under a cloth, and to one side the saint's shrine when it is on the island. The psalms go on at all hours in voices that do not hurry. Wax, damp wool and the sea.
sites.source: Timber, wattle and thatch; about 800 the wooden church replaced in stone: en.wikipedia Iona Abbey (no dig cited (?)). Whether the church burned in 825 is not known (dossier hi.md 8)

sites.name: The high crosses
sites.see: Four great crosses of stone before the church door, taller than two men, cut all over with bosses and snakes and, on one, the Virgin and Child among angels. One has arms so wide that they have cracked, and the masons have set a ring of stone round the crossing to hold them. Lichen is already at work on the oldest. Brothers bow to them going in; gulls sit on them going nowhere.
sites.source: Saint Martin's cross, 8th century, still stands where it was set; Saint John's broke for the width of its arms and the stone ring may have been made here to hold such arms; Saint Oran's and Saint Matthew's in pieces: Historic Environment Scotland; en.wikipedia Iona Abbey, High cross (the ring, from memory (?)). Some stone came by boat from Loch Sween

sites.name: The knoll of the writing hut
sites.see: A hump of bare rock facing the church, with a small hut of planks on its top, the door looking east over the Sound. This is where Columba sat writing with the door open, and where the abbot sits when he wants to be found. From the top you can see every boat on the sand and count the brothers in the fields. After the burning there is charred wood here and, in time, a socket cut for a cross.
sites.source: Torr an Aba: Columba's writing hut by Adomnan; dug 1956-57, charred wood and a socket for a cross (en.wikipedia Iona Abbey); charcoal dated to Columba's lifetime, published 2017, from memory (?). ask_omen here is a monk's reading of the weather and the birds, not a heathen rite

sites.name: The writing house
sites.see: A long hut with the best light on the island: a row of sloped boards, each with a calfskin leaf pinned on it, horns of ink, shells of colour, a goose wing for dust. On the widest board lies a page with one great letter on it and nothing else, the letter full of beasts biting each other, done so fine that it tires the eye to follow one line. A scribe breathes on his fingers. Skins stretched on frames outside, and a smell of lime and oak gall.
sites.source: A writing house and library: en.wikipedia Iona Abbey. The great Gospel most scholars hold was begun here about 800 and finished at Kells, not proved: 340 calfskin leaves; ochres, copper green, lichen purple, woad; no lapis: en.wikipedia Book of Kells (dossier hi.md 4, 8). The site closes when the shrine and the last treasures go to Ireland in 878 (the game's choice (?))

sites.name: The sheds by the ditch
sites.see: Three open-sided sheds against the inner face of the bank, out of the wind. A man works a pole lathe with his foot and a bowl grows out of an alder block; another draws a thread of blue glass from a pot no bigger than a fist; a third files a bronze pin. Leather offcuts and wood shavings go into the wet ditch, where they will lie a thousand years. Hammering, the creak of the lathe, charcoal.
sites.source: Wood-turning, metal-working and glass for windows and beads, perhaps from the 7th century: en.wikipedia Iona Abbey. Leather shoes and turned bowls from the ditch: dossier hi.md 2, from memory (?). The house-shaped shrine of about 750: en.wikipedia Monymusk Reliquary (that it was made here is not claimed)

sites.name: Oran's ground and the street of the dead
sites.see: A paved way of worn red stones runs from the shore between the fields to a walled plot of small crosses and flat slabs, each slab with a cross and a line asking a prayer for a man. Kings who came to die as pilgrims lie here among brothers nobody remembers. The grass is cropped by sheep. From the south bay, some years, a body comes up the paved way on six shoulders with a psalm going before it; after 806 there are sixty-eight new graves in a row.
sites.source: Reilig Odhrain, with a timber building of Columba's age found under it; the Street of the Dead: Historic Environment Scotland. The south bay as the landing of the dead and of the martyrs is tradition; the annal of 806 names no place (dossier hi.md 1, 5). Over a hundred early carved stones, some asking a prayer for a named man: from memory (?). Saint Oran's Chapel is 12th century and not here. No king's grave can be shown (dossier 8)

sites.name: The western plain
sites.see: Over the low middle of the island, twenty minutes on foot, the land opens to the west: a flat green plain of shell-sand turf, barley in strips, black cattle, and beyond it white beaches and nothing at all until the world's end. Brothers reap in a line with their habits hitched up. A brother stands apart watching the western sky, because a crane is expected from Ireland and the house has orders about cranes.
sites.source: The western plain where the brothers reap, and the cattle: Adomnan I.29 (?), as in dossier hi.md 2. The crane to be fed three days as a guest: Adomnan I.48 in Reeves (number not checked (?))

sites.name: The seals' islet
sites.see: A skerry of wet black rock off the island's end with a hundred seals on it, grey and spotted, the pups white. They are the house's own herd and are taken by count, as a farmer takes lambs. A lay brother with a club and a hide boat keeps the place; skins dry on a frame, and oil is run down in a stone trough. The noise is like a hall at a feast heard through a wall.
sites.source: 'The little island where our young seals are brought forth and nurtured', and the thief from Colonsay who hid under his boat to kill them: Adomnan I.33 (Reeves 1874, as quoted in dossier hi.md 2, 7; wording not re-checked (?)). Goods: seal_skins, seal_oil (goods_793.json)

people.name: Bresal
people.trait: Thirty years abbot of Columba's island: has buried kings who came to die as pilgrims, and in his last years sees the first sails from the north.
people.want: The island's peace; vellum and wine; word of Lindisfarne, Columba's daughter house, and of who there is still alive.
people.fear: A sail from the north, and that he will be the abbot in whose day the long peace ended.
people.voice: Few words, the blessing first; Irish, with Latin for anything that must be exact. Does not raise his voice and does not need to.
people.looks: Very old, small, the Roman crown tonsure (his house gave up the old Irish one in 716), an undyed wool habit, a plain staff with a crook, a book satchel hung on a peg behind him.
knows: who is of Columba's family from Kells to Lindisfarne, and which house owes which a book or a prayer
the kings of the Irish and of the Picts by their fathers' names, and which of them have asked to be buried here
what his protection is worth to a stranger: a standing in law, for a set time, wherever the saint is honoured
Adomnan's law, and who has paid its fines and who has not
what Columba is said to have foretold of the island, which he tells only to a guest who has come twice

ties.note: Lindisfarne was founded from Hi; the two houses pray for each other's dead by name, and Bresal wants the list of June 793
the same man in the spine's cast
the abbot who comes after him, at one remove; learned the running of the house under him
his guest-master for twenty years; the only brother who interrupts him
received him as a boy and set him to the writing house
the same person
a woman of the isles on the English kings' rock, sister of a brother long dead: she sends a cheese when any boat goes west, and he sends a blessing back
the monk of Tallaght who is making a calendar of the saints: has had Hi's own list from him by letter, and sends back corrections
the keeper of the church by the black pool, to which Hi once sent wax in a bad year; the debt is remembered kindly on both sides
the pilot of the Dee, who once took two of his monks up the river toward Lichfield with a book (?)

lines.greet: God's blessing on the boat and the men in her. You are from over sea, so you have no standing here until I give it. I give it. Sit.
lines.greet_again: The same keel. Good. Columba said kings of strange peoples would honour this place. He did not mention merchants, but I do not think he would mind.
rumour: Our daughter on the English shore was struck on the eighth of June. If you have been there, tell me who is alive. I knew them by their letters.
Thirty years I have buried kings who came here to die clean. They arrive with forty men, and leave the forty for us to feed.
I look north now before I look east. An old man should not have to learn a new habit.
lines.saying: Latin for what must be exact, Irish for what must be believed.
lines.farewell: Go on the ebb through the Sound. If you pass Lindisfarne, tell the bishop the mother prays for the daughter, and by name.

people.source: Annals of Ulster 801.4 (chronicle_793.json 801-bresal); en.wikipedia Abbot of Iona; spine cast.bresal (trait, voice and looks are the spine's). Columba's saying about kings of foreign peoples: Adomnan III.23 (Reeves 1874, from memory (?)). His birth year is a guess (?). The lines are the game's.

people.name: Cellach
people.trait: The abbot who moved the house: practical, counts hands and boats, and will not leave the island empty.
people.want: Timber, stone and safe hulls to carry Columba's books and treasures to Kells in Ireland, and men who come back for the next load.
people.fear: To be remembered as the abbot under whom Hi ended.
people.voice: Brisk; gives a blessing and an order in the same breath. Counts aloud.
people.looks: About fifty, strong, tonsured, sleeves rolled, a habit hitched up for work, a wax tablet with a building's plan scratched on it, monks carrying a carved stone behind him.
knows: every name of the sixty-eight, and where each lies
the road from the Liffey and the Boyne mouth inland to Kells, and who must be given a gift along it
what a hide boat and a wooden boat will each carry dry, to the chest
which kings in Ireland gave Kells and why it cost no battle
what is in the book chests, and which book must not travel with which

ties.note: Bresal's house, which he inherits after Connachtach; the spine's tie
the same man in the spine's cast
trusts the scribe to pack the books; the scribe thinks he packs them like fish
the boatman has carried eleven loads to Ireland and been paid in blessings and one cow
the steward of the church by the black pool lodges his men and his chests on the road to Kells (?)
the same person
the monk of Tallaght who asked, once and politely, to see what was in the chest for Kells
the ferryman at the hurdles pilots Columba's boats over the bar and will take no fee; the abbot keeps count of what he has not been paid
the fosterling of Daigre, who follows him as abbot in 814 and finishes Kells

lines.greet: Blessing on you. What is she, seven paces on the keel? Then she carries one chest and two brothers. Come up and I will show you the chest.
lines.greet_again: You came back, which most do not in these years. God reward it. I have another load and less time.
rumour: Kells was given us without a battle. In Ireland that is rare enough that I had it written down twice.
Sixty-eight. I can say every name. Do not ask me to today; I have a wall to raise.
People say I am leaving the island. I am moving the things that burn. The saint's grave does not burn, and neither do I.
lines.saying: Pray as if the heathen come tomorrow. Stack timber as if they come tonight.
lines.farewell: Keep the chest high, dry and aft of the mast. If she fills, save the brothers first, and do not tell them I said so.

people.source: Annals of Ulster 802.9, 804.12, 806.8, 807.4, 814.9 (chronicle_793.json 802-iona-burned, 806-iona-68-killed, 807-kells-monastery, 814-cellach-resigns); en.wikipedia Abbot of Iona; spine cast.cellach (trait, voice and looks are the spine's). His birth year is a guess (?). The lines are the game's.

people.name: Diarmait
people.trait: Fosterling of Daigre, abbot after Cellach, a leader of the clients of God: strict with himself first, and tireless on the road with the saint's relics.
people.want: The shrine safe and seen: in Alba when the Picts' king asks, in Ireland when the sea is bad, and on the island on the saint's feast.
people.fear: That the house will come to love its ease, or its gold, more than its rule.
people.voice: Dry and spare. Says the hard thing kindly and does not repeat it.
people.looks: In his late thirties, lean as a rake, tonsured, a patched undyed habit, bare feet in all weathers, a small bronze hand-bell at his belt and salt stains to the knee from boats.
knows: where the shrine is this season, and that he will not tell
the way of the clients of God: what they eat, when they fast, and what they think of ale
the courts of the Picts' king and of the kings of the northern Irish, and what each wants from the saint
who buys and sells Irish captives in the islands, and what Adomnan's law says they owe

ties.note: followed him in 814 and finished what he began at Kells
the same man in this file
the scribe travels with him to keep the list of what is carried
has crossed with him in weather neither should have gone out in
the monk of Tallaght who makes the calendar of saints in verse: both are clients of God, and they send each other feast days (?)

lines.greet: You are welcome for God's sake. There is water, bread and a bed. There is no ale in this house now. You will live.
lines.greet_again: The merchant. Sit. You look well fed, which I do not hold against a layman.
rumour: I carry the shrine to Alba and back to Ireland as a man carries a lamp in wind. One day somebody will ask why it was ever moved.
Blathmac asked my leave to stay on the island. A king's son, asking leave. I gave it. God forgive us both.
A Frank has made verses on our dead, I am told, beside some lake in the south. Our news travels better than our wine.
lines.saying: Mael Ruain said it: the liquor that causes forgetfulness of God shall not be drunk here.
lines.farewell: Go safely, and keep Friday's fast even at sea. The fish will not hold it against you.

people.source: Annals of Ulster 814.9; en.wikipedia Diarmait of Iona (relics to Alba 818 and 829, to Ireland 831; a leader of the Celi De). The year of his death is not known: 'to' is the last year he is recorded (?). Mael Ruain's words: The Monastery of Tallaght 6 (Gwynn and Purton 1911), as quoted in Design/content/peoples/irish_gaelic.md 9; the translators' death years not checked (?). Walafrid's verses: after 825 (?). His birth year and looks are guesses (?). The lines are the game's.

people.name: Óengus
people.trait: The brother who washes the feet, tastes the wine and asks the questions: round, quick, fond of talk and ashamed of none of it.
people.want: Wine for the altar, salt and iron for the house, and a guest with a year's news in him.
people.fear: An empty guest house; and, after 795, a full beach.
people.voice: Warm and nosy. Asks three things at once and remembers all three answers next year.
people.looks: Mid forties, stout for a monk, red-faced, tonsured, sleeves rolled above wet forearms, a linen towel over one shoulder and a horn spoon on a thong for tasting.
knows: what the house needs this season and what it can give for it: sealskin, seal oil, a turned bowl, a letter, a name said at the altar
what every guest of the last twenty years said was happening in the world
the law on strangers: who may stand surety, what a bargain needs, and why nothing is carried on the Lord's day
which pilgrims in the guest house are kings and which only say so

ties.note: speaks for the abbot in small things, and interrupts him in large ones
the boatman brings him the guests; he brings the boatman the leavings of the guests' table
wine or skins: every cargo starts the argument again
the cellarer of the daughter house; they have never met and have sent each other messages by ship for fifteen years
the same abbot in the spine's cast

lines.greet: Feet first, friend, then news, then food. That is the order of the house and I did not make it. Where are you out of?
lines.greet_again: I know those feet. Sit. The brothers wrote down what you told us last time, and I am to ask whether it was true.
rumour: It is a fast today. You are a guest, so it is not. The brothers are very glad to see you, for reasons of charity.
A stranger from over sea is a grey dog in our law, with no price on his face. Under the abbot's word you are a man again.
Sailors from Gaul used to bring the wine and the year's news together. Now the wine comes seldom and the news comes by itself.
lines.saying: Three signs of ill-breeding: a long visit, staring, constant questioning. I am allowed the third. It is my office.
lines.farewell: God before you on the water. Bring wine if you find it, wax if you do not, and yourself in any case.

people.source: invented; the office and the washing of feet from Adomnan I.4, the fast broken for a guest from I.20 (Reeves 1874, as in dossier hi.md); Gallican sailors bringing news, I.22 (?). The grey dog (cu glas): Design/content/peoples/irish_gaelic.md 5. The triad: Kuno Meyer, The Triads of Ireland (1906), as quoted in the same file. He is one of the sixty-eight of 806 (the game's choice).

people.name: Muiredach
people.trait: Second hand in the writing house: rules the lines, mixes the colours, writes the plain text beside another man's wonders, and has opinions about all of it.
people.want: Calfskin without fly-holes, woad, lichen, orpiment, oak gall, and the great Gospel finished before something happens to it.
people.fear: Salt water. Fire he has seen and can run from; a wet book is a thing done quietly, by a careless man with a boat.
people.voice: Quick, complaining and funny, like a note in a margin. Praises a thing by listing what is wrong with it.
people.looks: Mid twenties in 793, long and stooped, tonsured, inky to the knuckle, a quill behind one ear and a second in his hand, a cat-scratched wrist, lichen purple under his nails.
knows: what a book is worth and why: so many calves, a scribe's year, the colours, the cover
where each colour comes from and which of them a merchant can really find: woad, the copper green, red lead, orpiment, and the purple from the island's own rocks
what is in the book chests of Hi, Kells and Lindisfarne, and what each lacks
the verses scribes write in margins, and one about a bitter wind that he says he did not write
how to pack a book for a small boat, which he will show once and expects to be remembered

ties.note: came to the house as a boy under him
skins or wine: the argument is older than either of them
goes with the shrine as its clerk and comes back with the island's news of Ireland
the master of the daughter's writing house; they lend each other exemplars and blame each other for the errors
Alcuin's book-hunter has written asking what Hi has of Adomnan that York lacks (?)
one schoolman knows another: will lend the crew's reader a leaf to read aloud at anchor
the abbot has him pack the books for Kells; he packs them like fish, and Muiredach repacks them at night
has told the boatman how to stow a book so often that the man now does it wrong on purpose

lines.greet: Mind the door, the wind lifts the leaves. You carry skins? Calf, not sheep? Then you are the best thing to land here since Easter.
lines.greet_again: Ah, the merchant. The last skins were good. Two had fly-holes. I wrote round them, and nobody will notice for a thousand years.
rumour: The purple is a lichen off these rocks and the blue is woad. People ask for the blue stone from beyond Rome. People may ask.
The master does one great page in a season. I do the plain lines beside it. He is praised. I am legible.
Colum Cille stopped at the foot of a page and left the next to Baithene. Every scribe here hopes to stop at the foot of a page.
lines.saying: New parchment, bad ink. I say nothing more.
lines.farewell: Keep the bundle off the bilge boards. A wet skin is a drumhead, and I cannot write on a drum.

people.source: invented; a scribe is among the people the evidence shows (dossier hi.md 3). The colours: en.wikipedia Book of Kells (no lapis). Columba at the foot of the page: Adomnan III.23 (Reeves 1874; Design/content/lore/texts_more.json adamnan_last_page). The margin: an Irish scribe's note of about 850, Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II (Stokes and Strachan 1903), as quoted in Design/content/peoples/irish_gaelic.md 9. The bitter wind: texts_793.json irish_viking_terror.

people.name: Domnall
people.trait: A lay tenant of the house who keeps its boats: ferries pilgrims over the Sound, tows timber from the lochs, counts the seals, and knows every rock from the Torran reefs to Staffa.
people.want: A second wooden boat, tar, good rope, and a son who does not go to the Northmen for a wage.
people.fear: The Torran rocks in a southerly with a strange master at the helm; later, any square sail at all.
people.voice: Unhurried and exact about water, vague about everything else. Calls every foreign master 'the Frisian'.
people.looks: Late twenties in 793, short, wide in the shoulder, black hair cropped, bare-legged in a belted wool shirt gone white with salt, a sealskin cap and a wooden bailer hung at his belt.
knows: the marks through the Sound and round the Torran rocks, at every state of the tide
where timber is to be had on the mainland lochs and what the men there take for it
who is shouting from Mull, by the shout
the seal count, the weather for three days, and which skerries have a landing
after 795: where a boat may be hidden on the west side, and how long a long ship takes to round the Ross

ties.note: brings him guests and is fed for it
carried the house's chests to Ireland, load after load
the same abbot in the spine's cast
the scribe has told him how to stow a book so many times that he now does it wrong on purpose, once
the Dee pilot, met at the feast of Colum Cille, who brings lead and takes sealskin (?)
carries the abbot and the shrine between Alba and Ireland, in weather neither should be out in

lines.greet: You came in past the Torran rocks with nobody aboard who knows them? Then the saint likes you. Next time take me.
lines.greet_again: I saw the sail off Erraid and said: that is the Frisian, and he still holds too far west. Welcome back.
rumour: When a man shouts from Mull I can tell if he is a pilgrim, a debtor or a king. Kings shout once.
A man of Colonsay hid under his boat in the dunes to kill our seals. The saint sent him home with sheep. We still count the seals.
Timber comes over towed behind the boats, oak and pine from the lochs. This island never grew a tree a man could sit under.
lines.saying: The Sound is a mile wide and has drowned men who knew it. Do not know it too well.
lines.farewell: Go out by the south mouth on the last of the ebb, and give the rocks more room than you think is manly.

people.source: invented; a boatman at the ferry and seal-keepers are among the people the evidence shows (dossier hi.md 3). The shout across the Sound, the seal thief of Colonsay (Adomnan I.33), timber towed by boat (from memory (?)): dossier hi.md 1, 4, 7. The Torran Rocks and Erraid: en.wikipedia Isle of Mull, Sound of Iona.

people.name: Kali
people.trait: A Norse shipmaster of the islands, baptised like his father, who trades between Dublin, Chester and the Orkneys and comes to Hi because his brother is buried here.
people.want: A fair price for sealskin and marten, the going weight of the Dublin penny, and his brother's stone kept clear of grass.
people.fear: Dying somewhere the monks cannot find him to bring him here.
people.voice: Says less than he means and laughs after, not during. Norse with Irish words for everything holy.
people.looks: About thirty-five, fair hair plaited at the neck, a trimmed beard, a blue wool cloak pinned with a silver ring brooch of the Irish kind, a small cross and a small hammer on one thong, a folding scale in a pouch.
knows: who takes a share of a keel this summer between Man and Orkney: the earl's men, the Dublin king's, or whoever has ships
the weight and worth of English, Dublin and Manx pennies, to the grain
the Dee and its reeve: four pence a load and the king's first sight of marten skins
runes, and one old riddle about the giant whose bones are the hills
which graves in Oran's ground are of his own people

ties.note: pays King Sitriuc's man on the strand and carries his pennies north
has a new boat building in his yard on the Liffey and has paid half
a rich man of York with whom he trades marten skins and old questions; Styr has the third riddle (?)
the king's reeve at the Dee: four pence a load and first sight of the marten skins; Kali pays, and tells him the Orkney news

lines.greet: You lie beside me, so we share the watch. Kali, Olvir's son. I trade from Dublin to the Orkneys and come here to see a brother.
lines.greet_again: The merchant with the long memory. Sit on my chest; it is mostly sealskin now. What does the penny weigh in Chester this year?
rumour: My brother Fugl is under that stone. I had runes cut on it myself. The monks' letters would be strange to him.
North of here the earl in Orkney takes his share of every keel. South it is the Dublin king. Here, only the saint, who asks less.
My father's father came to these islands to take things. I come to lay a stone. The sea is the same. We got older.
lines.saying: Praise the day at evening, and the harbour when you are out of it again.
lines.farewell: Fair wind. If they ask you in Dublin about the giant's bones, the answer begins under your feet.

people.source: A rune-cut cross slab on the island, of the late 10th or 11th century, reads that Kali son of Olvir laid the stone over his brother Fugl: en.wikipedia Scandinavian Scotland; the names from memory, not re-checked (?). Nothing else is known of him: trade, years, looks and words are invented. Chester's dues: Domesday Book, as in Design/content/realms/irish_sea.md. The saying turns Havamal 81 (Bellows 1923; texts_793.json havamal_081). The riddle: riddles_793.json set ymirs_kin.

people.name: Feradach
people.trait: Abbot of a half-emptied island in the Northmen's sea: keeps the office going with a handful of brothers, and sends the saint's treasures out of reach a boatload at a time.
people.want: The shrine safe in Ireland; salt, wine and news; one year with no square sail in the Sound.
people.fear: To be the abbot who lost the shrine at sea, or the one who kept it on the island a summer too long.
people.voice: Quiet, exact, a little tired; gives the blessing in Irish and the list in Latin.
people.looks: About sixty, lean, a grey crown tonsure, an undyed habit patched at the knees, a small bronze hand-bell at his belt and an oak staff worn black at the grip.
knows: what is still on the island, and what has gone to Kells and to Dunkeld
how a shrine is packed for a boat: waxed cloth, hide, and two brothers who can swim
which sea-lords in the islands are christened, and which only say so
that Saint Cuthbert's people on the English shore are thinking of the road

ties.note: writes to the bishop of the daughter house how treasures are moved: what to carry, what to bury, and what to leave for God to mind
came to the island as a boy in the last years of Diarmait's wandering with the shrine (invented)

lines.greet: God's blessing on the boat. You find us few. Sit. There is water and bread, and I should like to hear what the sea looks like from the south.
lines.greet_again: The same keel, and still afloat. Then somebody prays for you. Sit down. I have a use for a dry hold.
rumour: The shrine goes to Ireland this year or the next. I have said so to the brothers. I have not yet said it to the saint.
A bishop on the English shore writes that he must leave his island with his saint's body. I wrote back what we have learned: carry the bones, bury the bell, and do not look behind.
Half the sea-lords in these islands have been dipped. They still take the cattle. They cross themselves first, which is a beginning.
lines.saying: A treasure in the ground is safe from men. A treasure in a boat is safe from nobody but God.
lines.farewell: Go on the ebb, by the south mouth. If you meet a sail with stripes, we have never met.

people.source: Feradach son of Cormac, abbot of Hi, died 880 (Annals of Ulster 880 (?)); in 878 the shrine of Colum Cille and his other relics were brought to Ireland in flight from the foreigners (Annals of Ulster 878 (?)). That he was abbot from 865 is the usual list (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbot_of_Iona (?)); his birth year is a guess. Made real in the weave of 7 Oct 2026 to answer lindisfarena.json's tie from Bishop Eardulf to 'the abbot of the mother house'. His looks and words are invented.

people.name: Thórir
people.trait: A Northman of the Dublin fort, carried out of it as a youth in the year the Irish took it, who washed up on the saint's island and stayed: baptised, tonsured, and still the keeper of one old question.
people.want: To end his days cutting the grass round the stones of his own people in Oran's ground; and that somebody should ask him the last question before he dies.
people.fear: That the brothers will find out how much of the old lore he still has by heart; and that they will not mind.
people.voice: Soft Irish with a Norse rasp under it; says a heathen thing and crosses himself, in that order.
people.looks: Big-boned and stooped, a fair beard going white, the crown tonsure, an undyed habit, a sickle for the graveyard grass in his belt and the white scar of an oar blister across each palm.
knows: the last question of the giant's line, which he gives on the sand and never on holy ground
which stones in Oran's ground are of his own people, and who lies under each
the Dublin hall as it was before the Irish took the fort, and who carried what out of it
the sea road from the Liffey to the Isles and on to the Orkneys

ties.note: the Dublin king's poet was a boy in the same fort; they have sent each other one question a year for thirty years
followed Hingamund out of the fort in 902 as far as Man, and left him there for the monks
the poet at York holds the question before his; they have never met, and each thinks the other's half the easier

lines.greet: God's peace. You have the look of a man who came for a stone or for a question. The stones are over there. The question I do not keep in here.
lines.greet_again: The merchant again. I prayed for your keel between two psalms. I shall not say which gods listened.
rumour: I was carried out of the fort at the black pool the year the Irish took it. We left ships half built. I have built nothing since but a wall round a graveyard.
The Dublin poet sends me a question each summer by some skipper. I send him the answer and a blessing. He keeps the one and laughs at the other.
My people come here now to lay stones over their dead, with runes on them and a cross. The abbot says the cross will do. I cut the grass round both.
lines.saying: The oldest thing a wise giant remembered was a boat. I think of that when the brothers read of Noah.
lines.farewell: Go safely. If they ask you in Dublin who keeps the end of the row, say an old monk, and that he is in no hurry.

people.source: invented: made real in the weave of 7 Oct 2026 to answer duiblinn.json's tie from the poet Arnfinnr ('a Norse-born brother on Hi, once of this hall, who still knows the last question') and this file's story hi.giants_bones ('whoever of that people is tending a grave in Oran's ground'). The riddle is riddles_793.json r-vafth-34 ('found: a Norse-Gael of the Isles', from 905). The foreigners were driven from Dublin in 902 (Annals of Ulster). Name: Thor- + -ir (names_placeholder.json Thorir).

people.name: Mugrón
people.trait: Successor of Colum Cille in Ireland and in Alba: a scholar and a maker of prayers, more often at Kells than on the island, who comes over for the saint's feast and for the dying.
people.want: The island kept as a place of burial and pilgrimage; kings who die clean; a quiet sea at the feast.
people.fear: The Danes of the islands at Christmas, when a house is full and its guard is down.
people.voice: Measured, courteous, a little grand; quotes his own verses and admits it.
people.looks: Sixty, tall, white-haired under the crown tonsure, a good dark cloak over the habit for the crossing, a bronze-headed staff, a small psalter in a leather satchel at his side.
knows: who is king at Tara and at Dublin this season, and which of them has been to confession
the houses of Columba's family in Ireland and in Alba, and what each owes the island
how a king is received who comes to die a penitent: straw, a grey tunic, and no title
what was agreed at the gate of Dublin after Tara

ties.note: receives the old king of Dublin as a penitent in 980, and sees him into Oran's ground
the ale-wife of the ford road at Dublin sends the island a cask each Columba's feast, for the old king's burying

lines.greet: God's welcome to you. I am here only for the feast, and for a king who has come to die. You find the island fuller than it has been in my time.
lines.greet_again: The merchant who carries without asking why. Sit. I have need of exactly that, and it is rarer than wine.
rumour: He was king at Dublin forty years, and twice at York. He sleeps on straw now, and asks what a slave fetches. I tell him to repent of asking. He does, and asks again.

After Tara the king of Tara stood at Dublin's gate, and every Irish captive in the town walked out free. I have had the day written into the calendar. Kings do so few things one can write down gladly.
I am told there are Danes in the outer islands again. The house will keep Christmas all the same. A feast one runs from is not a feast.
lines.saying: A king is received here like any other sinner. It is the only place he has ever been where that is a comfort.
lines.farewell: Go with the saint's blessing. If you pass the Liffey, tell the son that his father ducks his head at our door, and does it well.

people.source: Mugrón, abbot of Hi, 'successor of Colum Cille both in Ireland and Scotland', died 980 (Annals of Ulster 980 (?)); abbot from about 965 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbot_of_Iona (?)); remembered as a writer of verse and of a litany (?). Amlaíb Cuarán came to Hi in penitence in 980 and died there (Annals of Tigernach 980). Made real in the weave of 7 Oct 2026 to answer duiblinn.json's ties from Affraic and Sitriuc and its story duiblinn.open_gate. His birth year, looks and words are invented.

stories.title: The mother asks after the daughter
stories.summary: Lindisfarne was founded from Hi, and the two houses pray for each other's dead by name. Old Bresal has heard that the daughter was struck and does not know who is alive. A merchant who has been on the English shore can bring him the names, and carry back the one thing the mother can send: her prayer, a letter, and a word from the islands about which way the ships went home.
stories.picture: A very old small abbot on a rock knoll at dusk, holding a strip of vellum close to his eyes, a merchant standing below him with his cap in his hand, the Sound and the hills of Mull behind.

beats.text: Bresal asks what you know of Lindisfarne before he asks what you carry. He wants names: the dead for the altar, the living for his letters, the boys who were taken for both.

Higbald has the list written twice. One copy is for a king who may pay. The other, he says, is for the mother house, which will do the only thing that has always worked. (Sets lf_knows_boys if it is not set.)

The names are read at the altar on a fast day with the whole house standing. Afterwards Bresal gives the merchant his protection in writing, and Óengus brings a man of the outer islands who saw the ships pass north in June with their sails down, rowing for the fjord country.
The year of the first plundering. Bresal asks one more carrying: word to Lindisfarne that the mother has now been struck as the daughter was, and that the prayer has not stopped on either side.
Hunfrith the cellarer hears it out, says nothing for a while, and then pours for the merchant from the bishop's own jar. He has a message for a guest-master he has never met.

In a northern hall a man of the islands' speech is among the thralls. He knows the abbot's name and will tell a man under that protection what he would tell no other: which boys went where. (Helps toward lf_trail_north.)
On the English kings' rock an old woman of the isles, whose brother was a monk under Bresal, sends a cheese and a word about Easter by any boat that goes west.

endings.how: You brought the list from Lindisfarne to Hi while Bresal lived, and his answer back.
endings.text: The boys of Lindisfarne are prayed for by name on both islands until the last of them is home or dead. Bresal has the merchant's own name written after theirs, as one who carried.
endings.reward: The abbot's protection (flag hi_protected): a standing in law in every Irish and Pictish land that honours the saint. Bresal, Óengus and Higbald friendly at once. A letter worth a night's lodging at any house of Columba's family.

endings.how: You found one of the boys alive in the north and told it on Hi before telling it anywhere else.
endings.text: The old man gets up without his staff. Mass is sung at an hour when no Mass is sung. He sends the merchant to Lindisfarne on the same tide with a gift he cannot afford.
endings.reward: A small house-shaped box of bronze and yew for the merchant's own chest (worth about 90 d, not for selling); the abbot's protection; the feeling of every brother on both islands for a generation, passed to the heir at half strength.

endings.how: You came with the list after the summer of 801.
endings.text: Bresal is in Oran's ground. Cellach takes the list, reads it standing, and has the names added. He thanks you briefly and asks what your boat will carry.
endings.reward: The names are still read, and Cellach is friendly. No letter and no protection from this story: Cellach's must be earned by carrying.

stories.reward: The abbot's protection, friends on two holy islands who have never met each other, and a first word of where the ships went.

stories.title: The book of the four beasts
stories.summary: In the writing house a gospel book is growing that will take three hundred and forty calfskins and outlive every kingdom on the chart. Muiredach wants skins and colours for it. After the killing of 806 Cellach wants something harder: the unfinished book carried to Ireland in a boat, dry.
stories.picture: A single vellum page on a sloped board, one huge letter on it filled with knotted beasts in purple, green and yellow, a scribe's inky hand holding the corner flat, a small open boat seen through the door behind.

beats.text: Muiredach reckons the book aloud: the calves of a great herd, the years of four scribes, purple scraped off the island's own rocks. He names what a king's church would give for it and what a heathen would, for the cover alone. (Sets bk_knows_worth.)

The standing order, cut on a stick by the guest-master's boy: calfskin without holes, woad, orpiment, red lead, copper green, oak gall. Not the blue stone from beyond Rome: there is none in this book and none wanted. (Sets bk_parchment.)
Ceolhelm has a gospel exemplar Hi wants to compare, and wants a leaf of Adomnan in return. Each scribe warns the merchant about the other's carelessness.

Cellach shows a chest of oak lined with waxed hide. In it, in loose gatherings, lies the great book, a third of its pages still bare. He asks for it to be carried to the Liffey or the Boyne mouth, and for two brothers to go with it.

The chest goes ashore at the church by the black pool, where men of Kells wait with a cart and eight spears. A brother opens it on the strand before anyone is paid. (Sets bk_carried if the leaves are dry.)

News in Dublin: the great Gospel of Colum Cille was stolen out of the stone church at Kells for its gold case, and found under a sod months after, the gold gone and the book whole. An heir of the house that carried it is asked, by an old monk, whether the story in his family is true.

endings.how: You took the chest to Ireland and the leaves came ashore dry.
endings.text: The book is finished at Kells by men who learned on the island. Muiredach writes the merchant's name very small in a margin, in a place he says only a scribe would look.
endings.reward: 120 d in weighed silver and goods from Cellach, the flag bk_carried, the abbot's protection (flag hi_protected), and from 1007 an heir's standing at every church in Ireland that hears whose house carried the Gospel.

endings.how: The boat filled, or the chest rode in the bilge, with the book aboard.
endings.text: The leaves come ashore swollen and the purple has run. The brothers dry what they can on the strand, page by page, with stones on the corners. Some of it is saved. Cellach looks at the merchant once.
endings.reward: Nothing is paid and bk_lost is set: no house of Columba's family gives the merchant a book again until he gives one. The scribe's reckoning (bk_knows_worth) is kept.

endings.how: You would not take the chest: too dear a thing for so small a boat.
endings.text: Domnall carries it himself the next spring in the wooden boat, in three crossings, and it arrives. Cellach says the merchant judged his own boat honestly, which is more than most do.
endings.reward: No silver. The standing order for skins and colours stays (bk_parchment), at a fifth over the market, and Cellach stays easy with you.

stories.reward: The merchant can price a book in any market, sells skins and colours here above the market, and holds or loses the trust of Columba's houses with one crossing.

stories.title: Under the turf
stories.summary: In 825 word comes of a fleet in the islands. The shrine of Colum Cille is on Hi that summer. Blathmac son of Flann, a king's son who chose this house because it was dangerous, has the shrine buried under turf and will not leave. He tells the brothers who are afraid that there is no shame in going. A merchant on the sand has room for some of them.
stories.picture: A tall monk in a white vestment standing alone before a small church door at grey dawn, his hands open, fresh-cut turf laid back in place in the foreground with a spade lying beside it, square sails very small on the Sound.

beats.text: Domnall has it from a boat out of Tiree: long ships, more than five, working south. He says a long ship rounds the Ross in half a morning with this wind. The house has until tomorrow.

Blathmac speaks to the brothers after the night office. Those who can bear what is coming may stay. Those who cannot should go by the path they know, and not be ashamed. Then he asks the merchant how many the boat holds.
Brothers at the water's edge with nothing in their hands, by order. The boat can take them to Mull in an hour or to Ireland in three days. (Carrying them sets ms_carried_priest.)
Or the merchant can lie hidden on the west side with Domnall, boat hauled into the dunes under hay, and see what is done at the church, and be able to say afterwards that he saw.

Diarmait is back. The turf is lifted in front of the whole house and the shrine comes up clean. Blathmac lies in Oran's ground with the brothers who stayed. Diarmait asks the merchant to tell him all of it, once, slowly, while Muiredach writes.

A monk on the Rhine is gathering the tale for a young abbot at a lake in the south who makes verses. He has it third-hand from an Irish pilgrim. He would pay well to have it from a man who was on the sand.
The brothers who chose to go are lodged for a season with the clients of God at Tallaght, who write Blathmac's name among the martyrs and ask a merchant who was there for the day (?).

endings.how: You took the brothers who chose to go, to Mull or to Ireland.
endings.text: They come back in the autumn and bury the others. None of them ever says a word against the merchant or in his praise: he is simply fed, housed and prayed for on the island for as long as his house lasts.
endings.reward: The flag ms_carried_priest; free lodging and stores at cost on Hi for the merchant and his heirs; Diarmait friendly; the abbot's protection (flag hi_protected).

endings.how: You hid on the west side and watched.
endings.text: You saw them ask him for the gold, saw him answer, and saw the rest. You did not see where the shrine was, because you did not know. That is the part Diarmait asks about twice.
endings.reward: The witness's telling: 80 d and a bishop's goodwill for it at Mogontia, a place at the guest fire on Hi, and morale in your own crew hard hit for a season. The crew remember that you chose to watch.

endings.how: You put to sea when the word came and took nobody.
endings.text: Nobody blames a layman for it. The next time you land, the guest-master is a man you do not know, and he asks where you were out of in the summer of the killing.
endings.reward: Nothing gained and nothing lost but a year's warmth: every brother on the island is cool until you have carried for the house twice.

stories.reward: A place on the island that lasts past your own life, or a story no other merchant on the Rhine can tell.

stories.title: The old king's pennies
stories.summary: In 980 Amlaíb Cuarán, forty years a king of the foreigners, asks a passage from the Liffey to Hi to die a penitent. He brings a bag of English pennies as his gift to a house that has never struck or counted a coin. Six years later, on the eve of a bad Christmas, an elder of the house asks what should be done with it.
stories.picture: An old gaunt king in a coarse grey tunic sitting in the stern of a small trading boat with a leather bag on his knees, a low green island with one hill ahead, a monk waiting on the white sand.

beats.text: After Tara the town is full of men settling debts. An old man with ring marks on his wrists and two silent servants asks the price of a passage to Colum Cille's island, and pays it without haggling for the first time in his life.

Amlaíb gives the abbot a bag of some hundreds of English pennies. The guest-master has seen coin perhaps four times. He asks the merchant to weigh it and say what it is in ounces, and in cows. (A man with sv_scale is believed at once.)
The old king lies in Oran's ground under a plain slab with a cross on it. His bag is in the church, unspent: there is nothing on the island to spend it on.

Advent. There are Danes in the islands and the abbot, Máel Ciaráin, will not leave before the feast. An elder brings out the bag. It can go to Kells in the merchant's boat, or under a stone that only he and the merchant will know.
The abbot and fifteen elders died on Christmas night, the elder with the bag among them. Their killers were killed within the year. The new brothers have never heard of any pennies.

endings.how: You took the bag to Ireland before Christmas 986 and gave it up there by weight.
endings.text: The pennies are melted for a book shrine. Sitriuc of Dublin hears whose boat carried his father and, later, his father's silver, and has you to his hall.
endings.reward: 30 d for the carrying; King Sitriuc friendly, with first sight of his new pennies when he strikes them about 997; the abbot's protection renewed for the heir.

endings.how: You helped hide the bag, and after the killing you told nobody and took nothing.
endings.text: It lies where it was put, and will lie there. On the saint's feast the merchant, or his heir, sometimes walks past the place and does not look at it.
endings.reward: No silver. A vow kept: morale up in a crew that knows, and a thing an heir inherits that cannot be taxed, the knowledge of where three hundred and fifty pennies are, and the name of a house that left them.

endings.text: Some three hundred and fifty pennies, mostly English, a few of them cut. Nobody sees. Kali, years later, weighs one of your pennies on the beach, looks at the king's head on it, and asks no question.
endings.reward: About 350 d in old English coin, which a moneyer changes at a loss. No brother ever knows. The merchant does: the vow act is closed to him on this island for good, and the hoard that history records is not there to be found.

stories.reward: A king's son's friendship, or a secret, or a bag of silver: one of the three.

stories.title: The giant's bones
stories.summary: From about 905 the Northmen of the western sea are baptised men who still tell the old questions in their halls. One of the riddles of Ymir's kin is kept on Hi, by whoever of that people is tending a grave in Oran's ground; from about 995 that is Kali. The answers, set in order from Dublin, York and the island, point to silver an army left by the Ribble.
stories.picture: A flat grey grave slab with a ringed cross cut on it and a line of runes down its edge, a fair-haired man in a blue cloak crouched clearing grass from it with his knife, the hill of the island behind under a low sky.

beats.text: In a hall by the Liffey a man asks from what the earth was made and from what the hills. He will give the answer for a better riddle, and says the next question is kept by a man who goes to the monks' island to see his dead.

A Northman on his knees at a cross slab, cutting the grass back from the runes. He will not riddle on holy ground. On the sand, at evening, he asks: whose skull is the sky? And he tells you who in York has the third. (Gives one riddle of the set ymirs_kin.)
The third question, in a hall where a Dane, an Englishman and a Frisian can all be cheated in each other's tongue. The answers, set side by side, name a river and a ford.
A Dee pilot knows the ford: on the Ribble, a day north, where the people driven out of Dublin in 902 came ashore, and where an army buried its chest and did not come back for it.

endings.how: You solved all three and dug at the ford.
endings.text: Cut silver, rings and ingots and coin of five kingdoms, in what was a lead-lined chest. Not the whole of it: the river bank keeps most, for a later age to find.
endings.reward: Hack-silver to the weight of about 400 d; the riddles of the set marked solved in the chest; Kali, or the grave-tender before him, a fast friend.

endings.how: You solved them and sold the answers to a skald in Dublin instead of digging.
endings.text: The skald pays in a ring off his arm and makes the answers his own. For some years afterwards strangers in Norse halls greet the merchant as a man who knows things.
endings.reward: An arm-ring of about 120 d by weight; a welcome and the first riddle free in every Norse hall on this sea.

endings.how: You told the brothers of Hi where the silver lay and whose it had been.
endings.text: The abbot says that an army's chest is the price of somebody's church, and sends two brothers with a spade and a psalter. They bring back a tenth and give the rest to the poor of the Ribble, or say they did.
endings.reward: 40 d as the finder's part, Mass said for the merchant's dead for a year, and the abbot's protection (flag hi_protected).

stories.reward: A riddle for the chest, a Norse friend on a monks' island, and silver or a name at the end of it.

works.name: Stone for a high cross
works.what: A block for the shaft and two for the arms, quarried on Loch Sween and brought fifty sea miles by boat, with a ring of four curved stones to hold the arms at the crossing so that this one does not crack as the last did.
works.needs: The abbot's leave; a boat that will carry stone, or the hire of the house's wooden boat; the masons free of other work.
works.gives: A cross before the church that stands for the rest of the game and long after it. The giver's name is cut small in Irish on the base, with a prayer asked for him (remember, for the heirs), and the abbot of the day is friendly at once.
works.picture: Monks and two masons raising a tall ringed stone cross with ropes and a timber frame before a thatched church, one mason fitting a curved segment of the ring, a merchant steadying a rope.
works.source: The high crosses, 8th to 9th century; stone from Loch Sween; Saint John's cross broke and the ring may have been made here to hold such arms: Historic Environment Scotland; en.wikipedia Iona Abbey, High cross (the ring's invention here is likely, not sure (?)). The cost is the game's.

works.name: Timber for the burned house
works.what: Oak posts and pine rafters towed over from the mainland lochs behind the boats, a dozen at a time, to raise the church and the guest house again after the burning.
works.needs: The burning of 802 to have happened; Domnall or another boatman to tow; calm weather in the Sound.
works.gives: The guest house and the church stand again a season sooner. Free lodging on the island for the giver, and Cellach hears the merchant out on any matter afterwards.
works.picture: A hide boat and a wooden boat under oars towing a raft of long trunks across a calm green sound toward a beach where charred posts stand, monks wading out to meet them.
works.source: Hi burned by heathens, Annals of Ulster 802.9. The island has no building timber; oak and pine were towed over by boat (dossier hi.md 4, from memory of Adomnan (?)). The cost is the game's.

works.name: A watcher's hut on the hill
works.what: A turf hut and a pile of dry furze on the island's one hill, at the north end, with a brother's keep through the sailing season, so that a sail is seen an hour before it is at the sand.
works.needs: The first plundering to have happened; the abbot's leave. Before 795 nobody on the island sees the need.
works.gives: Warning: a raid on the island is known a day before it comes, so cargo, guests and the merchant's own boat are never caught on the sand. The watcher also calls the weather (wait_wind costs no day here).
works.picture: A small turf hut on a bare rocky hilltop, a monk beside it shading his eyes and looking north over a wide sea scattered with islands, a heap of furze ready to light.
works.source: invented in the period's manner: no watch is recorded. The hill, Dun I, 101 m, at the north end: en.wikipedia Iona. The years to stay out of the Hebrides, 794-840: Design/content/realms/irish_sea.md.

works.name: A stone house over the saint's grave
works.what: A very small chapel of stone and lime by the church door, over the place where Colum Cille was laid, with room for a priest, a lamp and two pilgrims on their knees.
works.needs: The relics to have been shared in 849, so that the grave is what the island has left to show; lime burned from shell sand; a mason from Ireland or from Alba.
works.gives: Pilgrims come in greater number, and with them news and small trade at the guest house. The giver may claim burial in Oran's ground for himself and his heirs (bury), which no silver buys otherwise.
works.picture: A tiny steep-roofed stone chapel beside a larger timber church, its doorway barely a man's height, a lamp inside, two pilgrims kneeling at the threshold and a high cross standing over them.
works.source: Saint Columba's Shrine: a very small stone chapel by the later church door, perhaps of the 9th or 10th century, by tradition over his grave: Historic Environment Scotland. Who built it is not known; the cost is the game's (?).

works.name: A slab in Oran's ground
works.what: A flat stone with a cross cut on it and a line in Irish asking a prayer for a named man or woman of the merchant's house, laid beside the paved way of the dead.
works.needs: A death in the house, or a wish to be remembered; the abbot's protection, since a stranger has no ground here.
works.gives: The dead of the house are prayed for on the saint's feast. Each heir who visits the slab gains a little of the old feeling the island had for the one before (remember).
works.picture: A newly cut grey slab lying in cropped grass, a simple ringed cross on it and a short line of letters, a mason brushing dust from the letters with his hand, sheep grazing among older stones.
works.source: Graves marked with small crosses and slabs; over a hundred early carved stones, some asking a prayer for a named man in Irish: en.wikipedia Iona Abbey; dossier hi.md 2, from memory (?). The cost is the game's.

ships.how: built to order over a month
ships.note: A hide boat on a wooden frame, made here by the house's own boatmen: ox-hides tanned in oak bark and sewn, butter on the seams, a short mast. She is cheap, light enough for four men to carry up the sand, and will go anywhere on this coast in summer. She must be kept greased and off sharp rock.
ships.picture: A dark hide boat turned over on trestles on white sand, two men stitching a new hide to her frame with a bone needle, a pot of grease beside them.
ships.source: Hide boats in Adomnan (from memory (?)); the boat of two and a half hides, Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 891; Design/content/peoples/irish_gaelic.md 6; ship_classes_793.json currach

ships.note: The house's wooden boat, oar and sail, of the kind Dal Riata levied by the seven benches. She tows the timber and carries stone and, from 807, the chests for Kells. Hired by the trip with her boatman when the abbot can spare her, never sold.
ships.picture: A long narrow wooden boat with seven oars a side and a small square sail, drawn up on rollers on a beach, a block of stone lashed amidships.
ships.source: Wooden boats under sail and oar in Adomnan (from memory (?)); the levy of two seven-bench boats from every twenty houses: en.wikipedia Dal Riata (Senchus fer nAlban)

ships.note: A four- or six-oared boat of the Northmen settled in the islands, clinker-built of pine and oak, sold on the sand by a family that has a new one building or a man to bury. Handier than a hide boat and dearer.
ships.picture: A small slender clinker boat with high curved stems lying on the sand beside a hide boat half her weight, a fair-haired man and a monk looking her over.
ships.source: Norse settlement of the Hebrides and Norse burials and a rune stone on the island by the 10th and 11th centuries: en.wikipedia Scandinavian Scotland. That boats were sold here is the game's (?).

sayings.text: Here, at the end of the page, I must stop; and what follows let Baithene write.
sayings.source: Columba's last words as a scribe: Adomnan, Life of Saint Columba III.23, ed. Reeves (Edinburgh 1874); Design/content/lore/texts_more.json adamnan_last_page

sayings.text: Three sounds of increase: the lowing of a cow in milk; the din of a smithy; the swish of a plough.
sayings.source: The Triads of Ireland (Kuno Meyer 1906), as quoted in Design/content/peoples/irish_gaelic.md 8

sayings.text: Three false sisters: 'perhaps,' 'may be,' 'I dare say.'
sayings.source: The Triads of Ireland (Kuno Meyer 1906), as quoted in Design/content/peoples/irish_gaelic.md 8

sayings.text: To go to Rome is much of trouble, little of profit.
sayings.source: An Irish scribe's quatrain of the 9th century: Kuno Meyer, Selections from Ancient Irish Poetry (1911), as quoted in Design/content/peoples/irish_gaelic.md 8

sayings.text: Bitter is the wind to-night, it tosses the ocean's white hair: to-night I fear not the fierce warriors of Norway coursing on the Irish Sea.
sayings.source: A scribe's margin, 9th century (Kuno Meyer 1911); texts_793.json irish_viking_terror. Said on Hi from 795, on any night of gale

sayings.text: New parchment, bad ink. O I say nothing more.
sayings.source: An Irish scribe's marginal note, about 850: Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II (Stokes and Strachan 1903), as quoted in Design/content/peoples/irish_gaelic.md 9

sayings.text: The abbot who forbade ale said: my monks shall not drink the liquor that causes forgetfulness of God. The abbot who allowed it said: mine shall drink it, and they shall be in Heaven along with yours.
sayings.source: Mael Ruain and Dublitir, The Monastery of Tallaght 6 (Gwynn and Purton 1911), retold from the words quoted in Design/content/peoples/irish_gaelic.md 9
How a learned Irishman opens his answer to any question (Meyer 1911; Design/content/peoples/irish_gaelic.md 8). On Hi it is said before answers that take an hour

sayings.text: Feed the crane three days and she flies home. Feed a king three days and he sends for his household.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on Adomnan's crane (I.48 in Reeves (?)) and the royal pilgrims of 778 and 791

sayings.text: A stolen seal is a meal. A given sheep is a neighbour.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on the thief of Colonsay: Adomnan I.33 (Reeves 1874)

easter_eggs.text: A brother on the western plain is watching the sky for a crane. If one comes down spent on the shore while the merchant is there, it is carried to a house, fed for three days and nights, and let go toward Ireland. The brothers say this has been the rule since the saint, who was homesick too.
easter_eggs.source: Adomnan, Life of Saint Columba I.48 in Reeves 1874 (chapter number not re-checked (?))

easter_eggs.text: The old white horse that carries the milk pails will, if the merchant stands still, put its head against his chest. The boy who leads it says it did the same to the saint on his last day, and wept. It cannot be the same horse. Nobody on the island says so.
By the grave is a stone the length of a forearm, worn in the middle. It was the saint's pillow. Pilgrims are allowed to touch it and not to try it.
easter_eggs.source: Adomnan III.23: his pillow was a stone, kept by his grave as a monument (from memory (?))

easter_eggs.text: In an old leaf of Adomnan the island's name is written Ioua, and the scribe's u has a hooked foot. Muiredach says a careless copyist will one day read it as an n and give the island a name it never had.
easter_eggs.source: 'Iona' is a misreading of Adomnan's Ioua insula, n for u: en.wikipedia Iona (dossier hi.md 1)

easter_eggs.text: Ask anyone how big the island is and the answer is: about five families. It is Bede's reckoning, a hundred years old, and the brothers quote it to visitors with some pride at being so exactly known by an Englishman.
easter_eggs.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.4 (dossier hi.md 1, from memory (?))

easter_eggs.text: Every guest is asked for news and a brother writes down what seems worth it against the year. The merchant who lands in the same year as a great event may find, a generation later, that a line in a book of years at Kells is in his own words.
easter_eggs.source: A year-by-year record was kept on the island to about 740 and the Irish annals grow from it: en.wikipedia Chronicle of Ireland. That the habit of asking outlived the book is the game's (?)

easter_eggs.text: In the ditch behind the sheds, among shavings, lies a spoiled wooden bowl with the lathe's core still in it, and a child's leather shoe. The turner says the ditch takes everything and gives nothing back.
easter_eggs.source: Turned wooden bowls and leather shoes preserved in the monastery's ditch (dossier hi.md 2, from memory of the excavations (?))

easter_eggs.text: A Frank at Dorestad or on the Rhine who has heard of the island at all calls it Eo, and thinks it is near Ireland, or is Ireland.
easter_eggs.source: Walafrid Strabo's name for the island in his verses on Blathmac (dossier hi.md 7, from memory (?))

easter_eggs.text: From 990, among the Irish cross slabs, one stone has its prayer cut in runes down the edge. A brother who cannot read it has learned what it says by heart, in case anyone asks: Kali, Olvir's son, laid this stone over Fugl his brother.
easter_eggs.source: The rune-inscribed cross slab from the island: en.wikipedia Scandinavian Scotland; the reading from memory (?)

unlocks.what: The abbot's protection: a stranger's standing in law
unlocks.how: Carry for the house once as asked (the names from Lindisfarne, the book chest, the brothers in 825, the old king's silver), or fund a work here.
unlocks.gives: flag hi_protected: in every Irish, Pictish and Dal Riatan land the merchant is no longer a grey dog. He may make a bargain with sureties, is lodged at any house of Columba's family (Kells, Derry, Durrow, Dunkeld, Lindisfarne), and a wrong done to him is paid for at a fixed price. Lasts the abbot's life; an heir must renew it.

unlocks.what: A known pair of feet at the guest house
unlocks.how: Bring wine for the Mass, wax or salt twice running as promised.
unlocks.gives: Free lodging (lodge) and stores at cost (provision) on the island; the guest-master's news before the guest fire's (ask_news); passes to the heir at half strength, as feeling does.

unlocks.what: Domnall's marks for the Sound and the Torran rocks
unlocks.how: Hire him as pilot three times, or tow timber with him for the burned house.
unlocks.gives: The house's ships pass the Torran rocks and enter the Sound at any tide without a pilot and without the risk card; hire_pilot here costs nothing; a hiding place for the boat on the west side in a raid year.

unlocks.how: Sit through Muiredach's reckoning of the great book and take the order stick.
unlocks.gives: flag bk_knows_worth and flag bk_parchment: parchment (calfskin), pigments and woad sell here at a fifth over the market until 826, and books can be priced in a heathen market.

unlocks.what: A scribe's verse for the chest
unlocks.how: Lie at the island on a night of gale in any year from 795, and visit the writing house in the morning.
unlocks.gives: give_text irish_viking_terror ('Bitter is the wind tonight'). The crew's reader can say it at anchor in bad weather: morale steadies.

unlocks.what: A leaf of Adomnan: the saint stops at the foot of the page
unlocks.how: Carry an exemplar between Hi and Lindisfarne dry, either way.
unlocks.gives: give_text adamnan_last_page, when that text is in texts_793.json (it is proposed in Design/content/lore/texts_more.json); worth a gift at any English or Frankish writing house that lacks it.

unlocks.what: A share of the seal count
unlocks.how: Be a known guest (hi.guest_bed) and bring the house salt for the skins.
unlocks.gives: buy_at_source at the seals' islet each autumn: seal_skins and seal_oil at the house's own reckoning, a third under what they fetch at Legacaestir or Duiblinn.

unlocks.what: Burial in Oran's ground for the house
unlocks.how: Fund the stone house over the saint's grave, or carry the brothers in 825.
unlocks.gives: bury and remember here for the merchant and every heir: a death in the house costs the heir less standing, and the feeling of the island passes on whole instead of at half strength.
